name: Puberty: what happens and when to get advice
summary: Puberty brings body and mood changes at different ages, and the NHS says a GP can advise if it seems early or late.
keyPoints: The pages found describe puberty as usually starting between about 8 and 13 in girls and about 9 and 14 in boys.
Girls typically see breast development first and boys a larger penis and testicles, and both have a growth spurt and may notice mood changes.
Sources define early puberty as signs before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys, and advise a GP appointment if it is noticed.
Delayed puberty is often hereditary, and the NHS notes that most cases are normal variation.
Childline (0800 1111) is free and confidential; in a crisis, 999 is for immediate danger, NHS 111 has a mental health option, and Samaritans is on 116 123.

body.heading: What is puberty, and when does it start?
body.body:
Puberty is the time when a child's body changes as it grows towards adulthood. The pages found describe it as starting between about 8 and 13 in girls and between about 9 and 14 in boys. The first signs differ between girls and boys.

Both girls and boys have a growth spurt, and both may notice changes in mood.

body.heading: What changes happen in girls?
body.body: In girls, the first signs are typically breast development and pubic or underarm hair. One NHS source says breast buds tend to first appear between the ages of 8 and 13. Girls also have a growth spurt, and the hips become wider. Periods usually start after these other changes have taken place.

body.heading: What changes happen in boys?
body.body: In boys, the signs include a larger penis and testicles, a deeper voice and a more muscular build. Facial and underarm hair and a growth spurt are also common. The voice can change unevenly, and may sometimes switch between very high and very low. One NHS teen health service also lists wet dreams, which are involuntary ejaculations, as a change that can happen in boys.

body.heading: How can puberty affect feelings and skin?
body.body:
Teenagers may have mixed emotions that shift quickly, and mood swings are described as part of going through puberty. The Healthier Together guide notes that the part of the brain that helps to regulate mood is still developing. A Cambridgeshire NHS page says emotions can feel intense and that teenagers may not yet have the tools to handle them. Early puberty can also affect how a child feels, because it can be hard emotionally to feel different from friends.

Sweat glands become more active during puberty, which can cause body odour, and extra oil in the skin can lead to greasy hair and spots. Acne is common in both sexes and is linked to hormonal changes, not to dirty skin.

body.heading: When do periods start?
body.body: Healthier Together says periods usually start around age 12, and a later start is not usually a concern. An NHS page says periods often arrive about two years after breast growth begins. The first periods are often irregular, and cycles can take 2 to 3 years to settle, according to another Healthier Together page. Most girls have regular periods by 16 to 18, one of the pages says. The NHS page on starting your periods covers what to expect, and this site has a separate guide to periods.

body.heading: What counts as early or late puberty, and who can help?
body.body:
The sources define early puberty as signs appearing before age 8 in girls or before age 9 in boys. They advise booking an appointment with a GP practice if early signs are noticed. Some children develop certain signs early but not others, for example periods before the age of eight with no breast development, and a GP appointment is advised then too. Early puberty can sometimes cause a child to stop growing sooner than expected.

Delayed puberty is described as no breast development by around 13 or no periods by 16 in girls, and no start by around 14 in boys. Another NHS source advises seeing a GP if periods have not started by 15, or by 13 if there are no other signs of puberty. Delayed puberty is often hereditary, so a child whose parent started late is more likely to start late too.

Sources also list puberty that has started but does not progress or stops abruptly, signs appearing in an unusual order, and slow growth as reasons to ask a GP. The NHS notes that most cases are normal variation, so a GP visit is often mainly for reassurance. Medicine is usually only recommended for early puberty if it is thought likely to cause emotional or physical problems. A GP may refer a child to a specialist if an underlying cause needs to be looked into. This is a routine GP appointment, not an emergency.

body.heading: Where can young people get confidential support?
body.body:
Healthier Together says Childline is free, confidential and open at any time for under-19s across the UK, and its topic pages cover puberty. Childline is free on 0800 1111, and the number does not show on a phone bill. Some areas also have confidential text services for young people run by school nursing or health teams, such as one in Derbyshire. A GP is the usual starting point when something is worrying but is not an emergency.

For a mental health crisis, the NHS says to call 999 if someone's life is at immediate risk. For urgent help that is not life threatening, NHS 111 has a mental health option answered by trained mental health professionals. Samaritans offers free support on 116 123 at any time.
